title: Vision system lighting techniques and filters
summary: Lighting choice controls contrast, glare, shadows, and repeatability in machine vision. Common geometries include backlight, bright field, dark field, diffuse illumination, multispectral lighting, and optical filters.
clean_markdown: Lighting is often the first variable to tune in a machine vision system. Use backlight for silhouettes and edges, bright field for flat reflective geometry, dark field for edges and surface texture, diffuse lighting for curved shiny surfaces, and filters or polarization when glare or color contrast matters.

title: Machine vision hardware components
summary: Machine vision hardware choices should start from the application. Camera, lens, sensor, lighting, processor, and software must work together rather than being selected independently.
clean_markdown: A vision system is a combination of sensor, optics, lighting, processing, and integration. The application should drive the hardware choices: required detail size, motion, contrast mechanism, field of view, working distance, and available installation space all matter.

title: Vision sensor components
summary: Vision sensors combine lenses, image sensors, lighting, processing tools, and communications. Lighting makes relevant features visible so image tools can process them reliably.
clean_markdown: Vision sensors and vision systems share common building blocks: optics form the image, sensors digitize light, lighting creates feature contrast, processing tools analyze the image, and communications return results to automation equipment.

title: Moritex machine vision lighting overview
summary: Machine vision lighting families include backlight, bar, brick, coaxial, and ring formats. Each lighting type is associated with different inspection use cases such as gauging, location, presence, or alignment.
clean_markdown: Lighting families should be matched to the inspection geometry. Backlights are useful for gauging and silhouettes; bar lights can be arranged for directional contrast; coaxial lights support flat reflective surfaces; ring lights provide compact front illumination for alignment and general inspection.

title: Backlight illumination for machine vision
summary: Backlights create high-contrast silhouettes and are useful for edge detection, gauging, holes, and shape inspection. They are usually poor for surface texture or OCR on the front face.
clean_markdown: Backlight is a strong first choice when the inspection target is an outline, edge, hole, gap, or dimension. The part blocks light and forms a silhouette. It is less useful when the feature is printed, textured, or located on the front surface instead of the contour.

title: Brightfield spot and bar light illumination
summary: Partial bright field with spot or bar lights can enhance surface features by changing the incident angle. It often provides more directional contrast than fully diffuse front lighting.
clean_markdown: Use spot or bar lights when the direction of illumination is important. Changing the angle can reveal edges, shallow relief, labels, or defects, but it can also create glare or shadows on reflective parts. Testing multiple angles is usually necessary.

title: Darkfield ring light illumination
summary: Dark field ring lighting uses low-angle illumination to make edges, scratches, texture, and surface defects bright against a darker background.
clean_markdown: Dark field is useful when small changes in surface height or texture need to stand out. Low-angle light reflects into the camera from scratches, burrs, edges, and texture while flatter regions stay darker. It is a common option for metal scratch detection.

title: Brightfield dome illumination
summary: Dome lights provide diffuse, multi-directional illumination and can reduce harsh reflections on curved or shiny surfaces.
clean_markdown: Dome illumination is useful when the object is curved, glossy, or hard to light evenly. It can suppress localized glare and shadows, but it may reduce contrast for shallow defects that need directional lighting.

title: Brightfield ring light illumination
summary: Ring lights provide compact front illumination and are useful when uniform light near the lens is needed, but reflective objects may show circular glare.
clean_markdown: Ring lights are simple and compact for general front lighting. They work well for many presence, alignment, and moderate working-distance checks. On shiny flat parts they can create glare; dark field, coaxial, or diffuse geometries may be better depending on the feature.

title: In-line telecentric illumination
summary: In-line or coaxial illumination through the optical axis can help reveal low-contrast flat surface features and through-hole inspection when paired with suitable optics.
clean_markdown: Coaxial or in-line illumination sends light along the camera axis. It is often considered for flat reflective surfaces, etched marks, transparent features, and inspection geometries where shadows are undesirable. Telecentric optics can improve measurement repeatability.

title: Common illumination types and polarizers
summary: Illumination selection includes geometry, wavelength, filtering, and polarization. Polarizers can reduce specular glare and improve visibility of surface detail.
clean_markdown: If glare hides the feature, test polarization on the light, lens, or both. If geometry alone does not create contrast, wavelength and filters can change how different materials absorb, transmit, or reflect light.

title: Imaging system resolution basics
summary: Resolution depends on pixel size, sensor sampling, lens performance, contrast, and lighting. Small features need enough pixels and optical contrast to be reliably distinguished.
clean_markdown: Camera resolution should be selected from the smallest feature to detect or measure, the required field of view, and the optical resolution of the lens. More pixels alone do not guarantee usable detail if the lens, lighting, or contrast is limiting.

title: Advantages of telecentricity
summary: Telecentric lenses reduce perspective error and keep magnification stable across working-distance variation, making them useful for high-accuracy measurement.
clean_markdown: Telecentric lenses are often chosen for measurement applications because they reduce parallax and perspective effects. They can be larger and more expensive than fixed focal lenses, so the accuracy requirement should justify the added cost and space.

title: A Practical Guide to Machine Vision Lighting
summary: Machine vision lighting selection depends on geometry, pattern, structure, wavelength, object properties, environment, and filters. The same object can require different lighting for different features.
clean_markdown: A practical lighting workflow starts with the feature to reveal, then tests geometry, wavelength, and filtering. Backlight, partial bright field, full bright field, dark field, diffuse, and structured lighting each create contrast through different light-object-camera interactions.

title: Machine vision lighting intensity and wavelength considerations
summary: Light output specifications can be misleading unless distance, geometry, wavelength, and how the object receives light are considered. Radiometric and photometric measures are not interchangeable for machine vision.
clean_markdown: When comparing lights, source wattage or lumens alone may not predict image contrast. Consider irradiance at the working distance, beam geometry, color or wavelength, exposure, strobe behavior, and the material response of the part.

title: Bright field lighting training
summary: Bright field lighting depends heavily on placement and angle. It is useful when the target reflects light back toward the camera and can be adjusted with ring, spot, or bar light geometry.
clean_markdown: Bright field is not one fixed product type; it is a lighting geometry. Adjust angle, working distance, and light shape to control reflections and shadows. For reflective samples, glare management may require changing geometry or adding polarization.

title: Dark field curved backlight concept
summary: Curved dark field backlight concepts can wrap low-angle illumination around curved objects and can be useful when silhouette and surface edge contrast are both relevant.
clean_markdown: For curved parts, a single flat light may not illuminate the edge consistently. A curved or wrapped lighting geometry can help maintain angular coverage. This note is technique context only and is not imported as an IOO product record.

title: CMOS rolling shutter cameras
summary: Rolling shutter reads rows sequentially. It can provide good sensitivity and value for slow or static scenes, but moving objects can distort.
clean_markdown: Use rolling shutter carefully when the part or camera is moving. Sequential row exposure can create skew or geometric distortion. For static objects, rolling shutter can still be suitable and cost-effective.

title: CMOS global shutter cameras
summary: Global shutter exposes the whole sensor at once and is preferred for moving objects or high-speed motion where distortion must be avoided.
clean_markdown: Choose global shutter when parts move during exposure, when the camera moves, or when geometry must be preserved. It helps avoid rolling-shutter skew, though exposure, lighting intensity, and frame rate still need to be designed together.

title: Lens selection white paper source
summary: Lens selection links sensor size, focal length, working distance, field of view, aperture, and resolution. The correct lens depends on both geometry and required detail size.
clean_markdown: For lens choice, start with field of view and working distance, then verify sensor coverage, focal length, pixel size, aperture, depth of field, and distortion. Lighting access and mechanical clearance are also part of lens selection.

title: Understanding image sensors
summary: Image sensor terms such as global shutter, rolling shutter, pixel size, and sensor format affect motion capture, sensitivity, and lens choice.
clean_markdown: Sensor selection should consider shutter type, pixel size, sensor format, exposure, quantum efficiency, and motion. Global shutter is safer for moving targets, while rolling shutter may be acceptable for slow or static inspection.

title: Sony Pregius global shutter CMOS overview
summary: Pregius-style global shutter CMOS sensors are designed to capture motion without the geometric artifacts typical of rolling shutter readout.
clean_markdown: Global shutter sensor architecture is important for moving inspection tasks. It should be evaluated together with exposure time, strobe lighting, interface bandwidth, and required frame rate.

title: Illumination for machine vision
summary: Machine vision image quality begins with the light. Lighting creates contrast, stabilizes the image, and makes automated inspection more reliable.
clean_markdown: Illumination should be selected from the inspection feature and material behavior. Compare lighting by geometry, wavelength, uniformity, intensity at working distance, mechanical fit, and control method rather than by product family name alone.

title: Fixed focal lenses for machine vision
summary: Fixed focal lenses are common in machine vision; field of view and magnification are determined by focal length, sensor size, and working distance.
clean_markdown: Fixed focal lenses are robust and cost-effective for many inspection tasks. Use field of view, working distance, sensor size, and required resolution to estimate focal length, then verify distortion, MTF, aperture, and mechanical fit.

title: Telecentric lenses for machine vision
summary: Telecentric lenses reduce perspective error and are useful for precise measurement. Selection depends on field of view, magnification, working distance, aperture, sensor size, and feature size.
clean_markdown: For high-accuracy metrology, telecentric lenses can provide repeatable measurements across part height variation. They need enough space, correct working distance, and suitable lighting access. Large fields of view can make lenses physically large.

title: What is industrial machine vision
summary: Industrial machine vision combines camera, optics, illumination, processing, and integration to make repeatable automated decisions.
clean_markdown: A machine vision system should be designed around the inspection goal: guidance, identification, gauging, or inspection. Reliable results require the right combination of lighting, optics, sensor, software, triggering, and mechanical stability.
